clue.text: Starch silly person dropped into sparkling wine

indicators.note: something dropped into a glass ends up surrounded by its contents

explanation.surface: Someone foolish has tumbled into a vat of fizz, or a starchy thickener has been tipped into the bubbly.
explanation.walkthrough: Cava is the Spanish counterpart of champagne; the fool lands just after its opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassava is a tropical root crop, and its flour, tapioca, is a staple starch in many cuisines.

clue.text: Workers entering place for tea and slice

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: tea is drunk from a cup
TU = trade union, a body of workers

explanation.surface: Staff troop into a café for their break and a slice of cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place for tea' looks like a café but is just the vessel; the trade-union abbreviation is a crossword staple for workers.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut something up is to divide it into pieces, which is exactly what slicing does.

clue.text: Seeing nothing wrong in being well-groomed

indicators.note: letters that are wrong are out of their proper order and must be put right

explanation.surface: Someone sees no harm in keeping themselves neat and tidy.
explanation.walkthrough: SOIGNEE is a French loan word, the feminine form of soigné, used in English for a polished appearance.
explanation.definitionFit: Soignée describes a person, usually a woman, who is elegantly dressed and carefully turned out.

clue.text: Face trouble, regularly stealing from balconies

indicators.note: taking at regular intervals means lifting every other letter and leaving the rest

parts.note: the even letters: second, fourth, sixth, eighth

explanation.surface: A cat burglar working the balconies of a block runs into difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face trouble' reads as a verb, to confront difficulty, but here it is a noun phrase: trouble with the face.
explanation.definitionFit: Acne is a skin condition producing spots and pimples, chiefly on the face, so it is literal facial trouble.

clue.text: Unearthly ordeal having to reorganise Dickens' work

indicators.note: reorganising means putting the elements into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A ghostly trial forces someone to rearrange a novel by Dickens, like a scene from A Christmas Carol.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dickens’ work' suggests a novel, but this is the weekly magazine he founded and edited from 1859.
explanation.definitionFit: All the Year Round was the literary periodical Charles Dickens owned and edited, serialising A Tale of Two Cities.

clue.text: Millenarian sect, mixers of cocktails

definitions.meaning: the American religious group awaiting Christ's return, named for their ecstatic dancing
the metal vessels bartenders rattle drinks in

explanation.walkthrough: Two unrelated senses of one plural noun: a religious movement and bar equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakers were an eighteenth-century celibate Christian community; cocktail shakers are containers used for mixing drinks with ice.

clue.text: Money temporarily put aside here for thriller?

definitions.meaning: the bookkeeping term for a holding ledger

definitions.note: whimsical: a tale full of suspense
definitions.meaning: read literally: a story told to keep readers on edge

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second sense as playful: an account, meaning a narrative, full of suspense.
explanation.definitionFit: In accounting, a suspense account temporarily holds entries whose proper destination is not yet known.

clue.text: Want to save money, so giving up the booze

indicators.note: saving something means keeping it safely held inside

parts.note: tin is old slang for money

explanation.surface: A hard-up drinker decides to go dry to cut costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' is the noun, meaning a lack, not the verb the surface suggests; tin is old British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Abstinence is refraining from something, most often alcohol, so swearing off drink is its commonest sense.

clue.text: Show old horse a single piece of tack

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H
the bit is the mouthpiece of a horse's bridle, part of its tack

explanation.surface: At a horse show, an elderly nag is paraded in a single bit of harness.
explanation.walkthrough: The equestrian surface hides that 'horse' is drug slang here; tack is a horse's saddle and bridle gear.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhibit is to display or put on view, a straightforward synonym of the verb.

clue.text: Bridge pair starting with spades concealing queen

indicators.note: something that starts with an item has it placed in front
to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: pr is the abbreviation for pair

explanation.surface: A bridge partnership opens the bidding in spades while holding back their queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The card-game surface points to bidding, but 'Bridge' is the definition: something that spans.
explanation.definitionFit: A spanner is anything that spans a gap, so a structure crossing a river qualifies in this literal sense.

clue.text: Complicated relationships get Mr Big at intervals into difficulties

indicators.note: to get into something is to go inside it
taking letters at intervals skips every other one

explanation.surface: A crime boss keeps getting drawn into messy entanglements, a gangster drama plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get ... into' is split, with its instruction wrapped around the fodder; 'Mr Big' is a gang boss, not a clue to size.
explanation.definitionFit: A love triangle involves three people romantically entangled, the classic messy arrangement between lovers.

clue.text: In brief, 'Academy' leads with a vowel

indicators.note: brevity asks for the shortened written form of the next word
something that leads goes in front of what follows

parts.note: an academy is a school, abbreviated SCH

explanation.surface: A news snippet reports that some academy is top of the league table, marked with a letter A.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a' is not a link: it supplies W and A after SCH.
explanation.definitionFit: The schwa is the neutral unstressed vowel sound heard in the first syllable of 'about', written ə in phonetics.

clue.text: Clutching note, place bet

indicators.note: to clutch is to grip, so one piece holds another

explanation.surface: A gambler clutches a banknote while placing a wager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place bet' looks like the definition, but 'place' is the outer piece and 'bet' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a punt is a small wager or gamble, and to punt is to stake money on something.

clue.text: Woo-hoo! Born during overlong time in bed? Refuse to go there

definitions.note: a noun phrase: the place where refuse goes

parts.note: whee! is another cry of delight

indicators.note: during means within the span of, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a lie-in is a long morning in bed

explanation.surface: Someone cheers a baby arriving during a lazy morning in bed, then refuses to go somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' reads as a verb but is the noun, rubbish; a wheelie bin is the British wheeled rubbish bin put out for collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Household rubbish is thrown into a wheeled bin, which is the destination for the refuse.

clue.text: One writes new title and a couple of pages in the bog

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

parts.note: a fen is marshland, a bog

indicators.note: something new has been remade in a fresh form

parts.note: pp = pages, one p for each

explanation.surface: An author drafts a new title and a few pages while sitting in the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the bog' tempts as British slang for toilet, but it is a marsh, the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A felt-tip pen is a writing implement with a porous fibre point, so it is a thing that writes.

clue.text: I present The End of History, a cancelled opinion

parts.note: 'here's …' is what a presenter says when introducing something

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A presenter introduces Fukuyama's book The End of History, an idea now widely rejected.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'The End of History' look like a title, which it is, but here it just means Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A heresy is a belief condemned by authority, and 'cancelled' is modern slang for being publicly shunned.

clue.text: One exploiting employees making garment

definitions.meaning: one who sweats workers, overworking them for low pay

explanation.surface: A boss who exploits their workforce is making clothes, a sweatshop scene.
explanation.walkthrough: To sweat labour is to overwork it for little pay, so a sweater is one who does so.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweater is a knitted jumper, and in older usage an employer who overworks staff for poor wages.

clue.text: A small train diverted to Nancy?

definitions.note: a definition by example: Nancy is one Sinatra

indicators.note: something diverted is sent off its usual course

parts.note: s = small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A little train is rerouted to the French city of Nancy.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy reads as the city in Lorraine, but it is the singer Nancy Sinatra; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Nancy Sinatra, Frank's daughter, sang These Boots Are Made for Walkin', so Sinatra is her surname.

clue.text: Is about to exclude a feature of browser

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way

parts.note: to debar is to shut out

explanation.surface: A web browser is on the point of removing one of its features.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is about to' reads as 'is going to', but 'about' flips IS and 'to exclude' is DEBAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A sidebar is a narrow panel down the edge of a browser window, showing bookmarks, history or tools.

clue.text: Tiny piece of high tech not fitting round a head

indicators.note: something fitted round another encloses it

parts.note: nob is old slang for the head

explanation.surface: A small gadget or helmet fails to fit around someone's head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not fitting' looks like one phrase, but NOT is the outer piece and 'fitting round' the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A nanobot is a microscopic robot, a hypothetical machine built on the scale of nanometres.

clue.text: Confront a constant expense

parts.note: c is the constant for the speed of light

explanation.surface: Someone tackles a recurring bill that keeps draining their money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constant expense' reads as one idea, a running cost, but it splits into C and COST.
explanation.definitionFit: To accost someone is to approach and address them boldly or aggressively, which is confronting them.

clue.text: Well up, holding firm in affliction

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within

parts.note: to well up is to rise, to surge

explanation.surface: Tears rise as someone stays strong through suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' is the noun, a business, not the adjective the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A scourge is a cause of widespread suffering, originally a whip used for punishment.

clue.text: Depression, given cereal that scours the teeth

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for 'stuff that scours the teeth'

parts.note: a dent is a hollow, a depression

explanation.surface: A gloomy breakfast of abrasive cereal that practically scrubs your teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' tempts as low mood, but it is a physical hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: Dentifrice is the formal word for toothpaste or tooth powder, which cleans by mild abrasion.

clue.text: State of mind turning to horrible fate

indicators.note: turning round faces the opposite way

parts.note: a mood is a state of mind

explanation.surface: Someone's outlook darkens as they contemplate a dreadful end.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's sliding mood fits the answer neatly: MOOD read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Doom means a grim destiny, ruin or death that cannot be escaped.

clue.text: When starting masseur falsely said he had a magic touch

indicators.note: what comes when something starts is its opening letter
something put falsely is set out wrongly

explanation.surface: A masseur boasts, untruthfully, that his hands work wonders.
explanation.walkthrough: The masseur's 'magic touch' sounds like massage talent; the definition is the whole last phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: King Midas of Greek myth turned everything he touched into gold, the original golden touch.

clue.text: Not old, condescend to pack it in

indicators.note: not having something means it is left out

explanation.surface: A young person refuses to talk down to anyone any longer.
explanation.walkthrough: One O comes out of STOOP. 'Pack it in' is British slang for stop or quit.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack something in is informal for giving up or ceasing, the same as to halt.

clue.text: Jazz work in theatre broadcaster half-heartedly takes on

indicators.note: takes on means adds the next piece onto the end
half-heartedly means half of the heart is gone: one of the two middle letters is dropped

parts.note: the Beeb is an informal British name for the BBC
an op is an operation, the work done in an operating theatre

explanation.surface: A broadcaster half-heartedly commissions a stage production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-heartedly' drops one of the two Es at the heart of BEEB, the nickname for the BBC. 'work in theatre' suggests a play, but the theatre is surgical.
explanation.definitionFit: Bebop is a fast, complex style of jazz developed in the 1940s, so a form of jazz.

clue.text: Stark nude changing clothes kept silent

indicators.note: clothes cover and surround whatever wears them
something changing takes on a new form

explanation.surface: Someone naked getting dressed says nothing about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stark nude' reads as one phrase, but it splits, and 'clothes' is a verb: the rearranged letters wrap around the synonym for stark.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unuttered has never been spoken aloud, so it has been kept unspoken.

clue.text: Came home missing river that's changed channel

indicators.note: whatever is missing has been taken away

parts.note: to come home is to return

explanation.surface: Someone returns without the river, whose course has shifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'channel' suggests a river bed, fitting the surface, but it means a TV or radio station.
explanation.definitionFit: To retune a set is to adjust it to a different frequency or station, switching what you watch.

clue.text: Police having time to replace cold headgear

indicators.note: replacing puts one thing in the spot another held

explanation.surface: Officers take a moment to swap their chilly helmets.
explanation.walkthrough: T takes the place of the C in COPPERS.
explanation.definitionFit: A topper is a top hat, the tall formal silk hat, so toppers are items of headwear.
